etymology: From hair, Saxon haer. In the Authorized Version the adjective identifies three men — Esau, Jacob's disguised hands, and Elijah — and once names the scalp of the man who will not stop sinning.
biblical_def: Esau is introduced by it: “the first came out red, all over like an hairy garment; and they called his name Esau” (Gen 25:25). The roughness is the man — the hunter, the field, the appetite that sold a birthright for red pottage. Jacob knows the difference between them exactly: “Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man” (Gen 27:11), and the deception turns on that single fact, so that the blind old father blessed the wrong son “because his hands were hairy, as his brother Esau's hands” (Gen 27:23). Isaac was deceived by touch after his ears had told him the truth — the voice is Jacob's voice — and Scripture leaves the reader to weigh a house in which everyone is manoeuvring and God's purpose stands anyway. The second man identified by the word is Elijah: Ahaziah's messengers describe the prophet who met them, “He was an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins,” and the king answers at once, “It is Elijah the Tishbite” (2Ki 1:8). John the Baptist wore the same girdle and came in the same spirit. And Psalm 68 uses it of judgment: God “shall wound the head of his enemies, and the hairy scalp of such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses” (Psa 68:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hairy as overgrown with hair; covered with hair; and notes Esau's description as the leading Scriptural instance.
webster_full: HAIRY, a. Overgrown with hair; covered with hair; abounding with hair.
HAIR, n. A small filament issuing from the skin of an animal, and from a bulbous root.
1. Collectively, a mass of filaments growing from the skin, and forming an integument or covering.
SMOOTH, a. Having an even surface, or a surface so even that no roughness is perceived by the touch.
scriptures: And Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man:
And the first came out red, all over like an hairy garment; and they called his name Esau.
And they answered him, He was an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather about his loins. And he said, It is Elijah the Tishbite.
But God shall wound the head of his enemies, and the hairy scalp of such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The adjective is descriptive and no framework has needed to bend it, though modern readers sometimes miss that the description of Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8 is a costume, not a compliment — a deliberate prophetic sign that reappears on John the Baptist.

The principle to recover is that God's purposes run through households as flawed as Isaac's. Every member of that family in Genesis 27 is manoeuvring: a father determined to bless against the oracle he had been given, a mother scheming, a son lying outright with his mouth full of his brother's name, and a brother nursing murder. The blessing lands where God said it would land before the twins were born. Scripture reports the sin without excusing it — Jacob pays for that morning with twenty years of exile and a father-in-law who out-deceived him — and shows, without a word of comment, that election does not wait on the decency of the elect.
roots_summary: Hebrew se'ar (H8181), hair; sa'ir (H8163), hairy, shaggy — also the name of Esau's land, Seir; chalaq (H2509), smooth.
roots_lines: Hebrew sa'ir (H8163) — hairy, rough, shaggy; Genesis 27:11, 27:23 — and the same consonants give Seir, the mountain country Esau settled.
Hebrew se'ar (H8181) — hair; Psalm 68:21, the hairy scalp.
Hebrew chalaq (H2509) — smooth, bare; Genesis 27:11, I am a smooth man.
Hebrew ba'al se'ar — a possessor of hair, a hairy man; 2 Kings 1:8, the phrase that identified Elijah at once.
Greek thrix (G2359) — hair; Matthew 3:4, John's raiment of camel's hair and leathern girdle — Elijah's sign resumed.
usage: “Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man”.
“He was an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather” — and the king knew him.
“The hairy scalp of such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses”.

pos: v. (past participle of shave: having the hair cut close or removed)
etymology: Saxon scafan, to scrape or shave. In Scripture the shaving of the head is never a matter of grooming; it is always a sign — of a vow discharged, of leprosy examined, of mourning, of shame, or of a strength forfeited.
biblical_def: Samson tells Delilah the whole secret in one sentence: “There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother's womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man” (Jdg 16:17). The strength was never in the hair; the hair was the sign of a vow, and losing the sign meant he had let go the thing signified. But the chapter ends with a sentence of mercy so quiet it is easy to miss: “Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven” (Jdg 16:22). At the far end of the vow, the priest took the ram's shoulder and the unleavened cake and put them into the Nazarite's hands “after the hair of his separation is shaven” (Num 6:19) — the shaving there is completion, not disgrace. Leviticus 13:33 uses it clinically, of the man with a scall shut up for examination. Jeremiah 41:5 shows fourscore men with beards shaven and clothes rent, coming with offerings to a house that was already burned. And Paul reasons from the shame of a shaven woman in his argument about head covering (1Co 11:5-6), which is the only New Testament use.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shave as to cut or pare off something from the surface by a razor; and shaven as having the beard or hair cut close.
webster_full: SHAVE, v.t. To cut or pare off something from the surface of a body by a razor or other edged instrument.
1. To cut off the hair from the face or other part of the body with a razor.
SHAVEN, pp. Pared; made smooth with a razor; having the hair or beard cut close.
RAZOR, n. An instrument for shaving off beard or hair.
scriptures: That he told her all his heart, and said unto her, There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother's womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man.
Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven.
Num 6:19

And the priest shall take the sodden shoulder of the ram, and one unleavened cake out of the basket, and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them upon the hands of the Nazarite, after the hair of his separation is shaven:
For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered.
corruption_summary: Samson's hair is read as a magic charm; Scripture makes it the sign of a vow he had been discarding for chapters.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular telling makes the hair itself the source of the strength, which turns the story into folklore and hides its point. The Nazarite vow had three marks — no wine, no touching the dead, no razor — and Samson had broken the first two long before Delilah. He feasted seven days with the Philistines, took honey out of a lion's carcase, and handled the jawbone of an ass. By chapter 16 only the outward sign was left, and when he gave that away the text says something more solemn than that his hair was gone: he wist not that the LORD was departed from him. The strength was the LORD's and always had been.

The other half is the mercy, and it must be preached with the warning. Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again — a blind man grinding in a prison house, and God quietly beginning again. Samson stands in Hebrews 11 among those who through faith subdued kingdoms, which no reader of Judges would have predicted. That is not an excuse for the ruinous years; the eyes were never restored. But it is the reason a man who has thrown away everything but the sign should not conclude that God has finished with him.
roots_summary: Hebrew galach (H1548), to shave, to make bald; nazir (H5139), one separated, a Nazarite; Greek xurao (G3587), to shave.
roots_lines: Hebrew galach (H1548) — to shave, to shear; Judges 16:17, 16:22, Numbers 6:19, Leviticus 13:33.
Hebrew nazir (H5139) — one separated, consecrated, a Nazarite; the vow of Numbers 6 and Samson's from the womb.
Hebrew ta'ar (H8593) — a razor; there hath not come a razor upon mine head.
Hebrew nezer (H5145) — separation, consecration, and also a crown or diadem — the same word for the Nazarite's hair and the high priest's golden plate.
Greek xurao (G3587) — to shave; 1 Corinthians 11:5-6, Acts 21:24.
usage: “If I be shaven, then my strength will go from me” — the sign, not the source.
“Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again”.
“After the hair of his separation is shaven” — a vow completed, not disgraced.

pos: adj. (hoary; white with age — in Scripture almost always of hairs and of a head)
etymology: Saxon graeg. In the Authorized Version the word appears almost exclusively in the phrase gray hairs or the gray head, and it is a moral word: age is either a crown to be honoured or a grief to be brought down with sorrow to the grave.
biblical_def: “The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head” (Pro 20:29). The proverb refuses to rank them; each season has its own proper glory, and an old man trying to keep the young man's has traded a beauty for a memory. Leviticus makes the honour a command — thou shalt rise up before the hoary head — and the whole biblical order of eldership presumes it. Jacob supplies the counter-image, repeated three times in the Joseph narrative as an old man's dread: “then shall ye bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave” (Gen 42:38), and again in the mouth of Judah pleading for Benjamin (Gen 44:29, 31). To bring a father's gray hairs down with sorrow is Scripture's picture of what a family's sin does to the generation above it. Deuteronomy 32:25 shows judgment sparing no age: the sword destroys “both the young man and the virgin, the suckling also with the man of gray hairs.” And Hosea gives the saddest use, of a nation in decline that cannot see it: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knoweth it not: yea, gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not” (Hos 7:9). A people can be visibly aging and wholly unaware.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gray as white with a mixture of black; and specifically, white or hoary with age; and gives the gray head as the mark of old age.
webster_full: GRAY, a. White with a mixture of black; hoary.
1. White or hoary with age; as a gray head.
2. Dark; of a mixed color; of the color of ashes.
HOARY, a. White or whitish; white or gray with age; as hoary hairs; a hoary head.
scriptures: The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head.

And he said, My son shall not go down with you; for his brother is dead, and he is left alone: if mischief befall him by the way in the which ye go, then shall ye bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.
Hos 7:9
Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knoweth it not: yea, gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not.
The sword without, and terror within, shall destroy both the young man and the virgin, the suckling also with the man of gray hairs.
corruption_summary: Age is treated as a defect to be concealed; Scripture calls the gray head a beauty and commands that men rise before it.
corruption_paragraphs: A civilization that spends heavily to hide gray hair has already announced its judgment on age, and the church has largely absorbed it — ministries built for the young, elders chosen for energy, the aged relocated out of sight and out of the assembly. Proverbs 20:29 assigns each season its own glory and gives the older the word beauty. Leviticus 19:32 makes it a matter of the fear of God: thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD. The command to stand is attached directly to the fear of God, which means contempt for the aged is treated as a species of irreligion.

Hosea supplies the warning that keeps this from sentimentality. Gray hairs are on Ephraim and he knoweth not. Age brings honour only where it has brought wisdom; it can equally bring an unnoticed decay, a strength devoured by strangers while the man believes himself unchanged. Both the individual and the church can reach that state. The remedy is the same in either case: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
roots_summary: Hebrew seybah (H7872), hoary head, old age; tiph'ereth (H8597), beauty, glory; she'ol (H7585), the grave.
roots_lines: Hebrew seybah (H7872) — grey hair, hoary head, old age; Genesis 42:38, Proverbs 20:29, Hosea 7:9.
Hebrew tiph'ereth (H8597) — beauty, glory, adornment; Proverbs 20:29, the beauty of old men.
Hebrew yagon (H3015) — grief, sorrow; Genesis 42:38, brought down with sorrow to the grave.
Hebrew she'ol (H7585) — the grave, the unseen state of the dead; the place Jacob feared to reach in grief.
Hebrew zaqen (H2205) — old, aged, an elder; the office in Israel took its name from the age.
usage: “The beauty of old men is the gray head” — a beauty, not a defect.
“Bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave” — three times in one narrative.
“Gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not”.

pos: adj. (stripped; made bare, of skin, hair or bark)
etymology: From peel, Latin pilare, to strip of hair. The Authorized Version uses it of a nation stripped bare and of shoulders rubbed raw — in both cases a people or an army worn down to nothing by long labour.
biblical_def: Isaiah's burden concerning the land shadowing with wings describes a people twice as “scattered and peeled” — first in the summons to the swift messengers (Isa 18:2), and then, remarkably, in the promise: “In that time shall the present be brought unto the LORD of hosts of a people scattered and peeled… to the place of the name of the LORD of hosts, the mount Zion” (Isa 18:7). A nation meted out and trodden down, stripped bare, whose land the rivers have spoiled, is nonetheless described as bringing a present to Zion. The gospel goes to the peeled peoples, and they come. The second use is Ezekiel's and is one of the strangest passages in the prophets: Nebuchadnezzar “caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus: every head was made bald, and every shoulder was peeled: yet had he no wages, nor his army, for Tyrus, for the service that he had served against it” (Eze 29:18). Thirteen years of siege; helmets wore the hair off their heads and the carrying of timber rubbed their shoulders raw; and the city, being an island, evacuated its wealth by sea. So God gives him Egypt as his wages, “for they wrought for me, saith the Lord GOD.” A pagan army is paid by the LORD for labour it never knew it was doing for Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines peel as to strip off skin, bark or rind; to flay; and peeled as stripped of skin, bark or covering; plundered.
webster_full: PEEL, v.t. To strip off skin, bark or rind; to flay; to decorticate.
1. To strip; to plunder; as, to peel a country.
PEELED, pp. Stripped of skin, bark or rind; plundered.
GALL, v.t. To fret and wear away by friction; to hurt or break the skin by rubbing.
scriptures: Son of man, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus: every head was made bald, and every shoulder was peeled: yet had he no wages, nor his army, for Tyrus, for the service that he had served against it:
Isa 18:2

That sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters, saying, Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation scattered and peeled, to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation meted out and trodden down, whose land the rivers have spoiled!
Isa 18:7

In that time shall the present be brought unto the LORD of hosts of a people scattered and peeled, and from a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation meted out and trodden under foot, whose land the rivers have spoiled, to the place of the name of the LORD of hosts, the mount Zion.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is descriptive, and its difficulty for a modern reader is archaism rather than distortion: peeled in Isaiah 18 means stripped or made smooth, not sunburnt or flayed in the modern sense.

The principle to recover is the doctrine of providence at its widest reach. Ezekiel 29:18-20 says that a Babylonian army besieging a Phoenician city for thirteen years, for its own imperial reasons, with no reference to the God of Israel, was in fact working for Him — they wrought for me, saith the Lord GOD — and would be paid in the wealth of Egypt. Kings and armies who neither know nor acknowledge God are nevertheless His instruments and are recompensed on His books. That is the same providence which the believer trusts in far smaller matters, and it is the reason Scripture can say that all things work together for good to them that love God.
roots_summary: Hebrew marat (H4803), to make bare, to pluck off hair, to polish; maraq, to scour; sakar (H7939), wages.
roots_lines: Hebrew marat (H4803) — to pluck out hair, to make bald or bare, to polish smooth; Isaiah 18:2, 18:7, Ezekiel 29:18.
Hebrew qav qav — line upon line, meted out; Isaiah 18:2, of the nation measured off.
Hebrew sakar (H7939) — hire, wages; Ezekiel 29:18-19, the wages Nebuchadnezzar had not received and would receive.
Hebrew qarach (H7139) — to make bald; every head was made bald under the helmets.
Hebrew 'abodah (H5656) — service, labour; the great service served against Tyre.
usage: “Every head was made bald, and every shoulder was peeled” — thirteen years of siege.
“A nation scattered and peeled” — and they bring a present to Zion.
“Yet had he no wages” — so the LORD paid him in Egypt.

pos: v. (past tense of stick: fixed fast; adhered)
etymology: Past tense of stick, Saxon stician, to pierce or fasten. Its three occurrences are a spear in the ground, a ship on a sandbar, and a man's soul cleaving to the testimonies of God.
biblical_def: “I have stuck unto thy testimonies: O LORD, put me not to shame” (Psa 119:31). It is a homely verb for a great thing — the same word one would use of a burr on a coat — and the psalmist chooses it deliberately. He does not say he has admired the testimonies or agreed with them; he has adhered to them, and the prayer that follows is the prayer of a man who has staked his reputation on a book: put me not to shame. Perseverance in Scripture usually looks like this rather than like heroism. The other two uses are pictures of being fixed fast for good or ill. Saul lay sleeping in the trench “and his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster” (1Sa 26:7) — the same spear he had twice thrown at David, now planted beside a sleeping king with David standing over him and Abishai begging leave to strike once. David would not stretch out his hand against the LORD's anointed. And Paul's shipwreck: “they ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves” (Act 27:41). The vessel held at the bow and broke at the stern, and every soul came safe to land exactly as the angel had promised.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stick as to adhere, to cleave, to abide firmly; and stuck as fastened, or having adhered.
webster_full: STICK, v.i. To adhere; to cleave; to hold to; as, glue sticks to the fingers.
1. To be constant or persevering; to adhere closely; as, to stick to a friend.
2. To stop; to be impeded; as, the boat stuck in the mud.
STICK, v.t. To pierce; to stab; to fasten by piercing.
scriptures: I have stuck unto thy testimonies: O LORD, put me not to shame.
So David and Abishai came to the people by night: and, behold, Saul lay sleeping within the trench, and his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster: but Abner and the people lay round about him.
And falling into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves.
corruption_summary: Fidelity to a fixed text is now called rigidity; the psalmist calls it sticking, and asks not to be shamed for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The word for a man who holds an unchanging standard is now rigid, and the virtue on offer instead is flexibility — a faith that moves with the times and is therefore always defensible in them. Psalm 119:31 is the other posture: a man who has stuck to the testimonies and knows perfectly well it may cost him. His prayer is not that he might be proved clever but that God would not let him be ashamed — which is to say that the whole weight of his standing is on whether the word is true. That is not rigidity; it is trust that has consequences.

The scene at Saul's bolster shows what sticking to a testimony costs in practice. David had every argument on his side: an anointing, a persecutor asleep, a spear ready to hand, and a friend urging him. He had the means, the motive and the opportunity, and he had a word from God he would not cross — who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD's anointed, and be guiltless? Fidelity is nearly always tested at the moment when disobedience would obviously work.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabaq (H1692), to cleave, cling, adhere; 'edah / 'eduth (H5713, H5715), testimony; Greek ereido (G2043), to fix firmly.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabaq (H1692) — to cling, cleave, stick fast; Psalm 119:31 — the same verb as Genesis 2:24, a man shall cleave unto his wife, and Ruth 1:14, Ruth clave unto her.
Hebrew 'edah (H5713) — testimony, witness; the plural testimonies that Psalm 119 returns to twenty-three times.
Hebrew ma'akah — the place at the head, the bolster; 1 Samuel 26:7, where the spear stood.
Greek ereido (G2043) — to prop, to fix firmly; Acts 27:41, the forepart stuck fast — its only New Testament occurrence.
Greek asaleutos (G761) — unmoveable; Acts 27:41, and Hebrews 12:28, a kingdom which cannot be moved.
usage: “I have stuck unto thy testimonies” — a homely verb for perseverance.
“His spear stuck in the ground at his bolster” — and David would not touch it.
“The forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable” — and all came safe to land.

pos: v. (torn open; in the Authorized Version, of women with child in war)
etymology: Of Northern origin, to tear or cut open lengthwise. Every occurrence in Scripture is the same atrocity, named three times by three writers: the cutting open of pregnant women by an invading army.
biblical_def: Three verses, one crime. Menahem of Israel “smote Tiphsah, and all that were therein, and the coasts thereof from Tirzah: because they opened not to him, therefore he smote it; and all the women therein that were with child he ripped up” (2Ki 15:16). Hosea prophesies the same thing coming upon Samaria in her turn: “their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up” (Hos 13:16) — the nation that did it will have it done to her. And Amos makes it the ground of a specific judgment on a specific nation: “For three transgressions of the children of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border” (Amo 1:13). Note the stated motive: that they might enlarge their border. The unborn were destroyed for territory — killed because a nation wanted room. Scripture places this among the transgressions for which God turns away no punishment, and it does so without any argument about when life begins, because none is required: the woman is with child, and the child is the one killed. That the Bible names this atrocity three separate times, in the histories, the prophets and the oracles against the nations, is itself a testimony.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rip as to separate by cutting or tearing; to tear or cut open; and ripped as torn or cut open.
webster_full: RIP, v.t. To separate by cutting or tearing; to tear or cut open or off.
1. To take out or away by cutting or tearing.
2. To tear up for search or disclosure; to search to the bottom.
RIPPED, pp. Torn or cut open or off.
scriptures: Amo 1:13

Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of the children of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border:
Samaria shall become desolate; for she hath rebelled against her God: they shall fall by the sword: their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up.

Then Menahem smote Tiphsah, and all that were therein, and the coasts thereof from Tirzah: because they opened not to him, therefore he smote it; and all the women therein that were with child he ripped up.
corruption_summary: The unborn are reclassified as tissue and their destruction as a right; Amos names the killing of the unborn as a transgression God will not turn away.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 1:13 is one of the most direct statements in Scripture about the unborn, and it is usually passed over. God announces judgment on Ammon for ripping up the women with child of Gilead, and the reason given is that they did it that they might enlarge their border — the destruction of children in the womb for the convenience and advantage of those who wanted the space. The prophet does not argue for the humanity of the unborn; he assumes it, as does the whole of Scripture, which knows men by name and calling before they are born (Jer 1:5), and describes David's substance as seen by God while it was yet unperfect (Psa 139:16).

The modern practice differs from Ammon's in method and in scale, not in the thing done or in the reason given. The category by which the child is excluded from protection — unwanted, unviable, not yet a person — is a redefinition, and redefinition is how every such killing has always been licensed. The church's duty here is twofold and must not be halved: to name the thing plainly as Amos does, and to receive with the full mercy of the gospel every woman and man who has done it and comes to Christ. There is no sin here beyond the blood of the Lamb, and the church that cannot say both sentences has failed at one end or the other.
roots_summary: Hebrew baqa' (H1234), to cleave, split open, rip up; harah (H2030), with child, pregnant; gebul (H1366), border.
roots_lines: Hebrew baqa' (H1234) — to cleave, split, rip open; 2 Kings 15:16, Hosea 13:16, Amos 1:13 — the same verb used of the Red Sea being divided.
Hebrew harah (H2030) — pregnant, with child; the women named in all three verses.
Hebrew gebul (H1366) — border, territory, boundary; Amos 1:13, the stated motive — that they might enlarge their border.
Hebrew pesha' (H6588) — transgression, rebellion; the word counted three and four times in the oracles against the nations.
Hebrew yatsar (H3335) — to form, to fashion; Jeremiah 1:5, before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee.
usage: “That they might enlarge their border” — the motive Amos records.
“Their women with child shall be ripped up” — done by Samaria, and done to her.
“All the women therein that were with child he ripped up” — a king of Israel.

pos: v. (past tense and participle of sink: gone down; settled into)
etymology: Saxon sincan. In the Authorized Version things sink into forehead, into mire, into a pit of one's own digging, and into sleep — and the verb usually marks the moment a matter is settled.
biblical_def: “David put his hand in his bag, and took thence a stone, and slang it, and smote the Philistine in his forehead, that the stone sunk into his forehead; and he fell upon his face to the earth” (1Sa 17:49). The champion who had defied the armies of the living God for forty days was settled by one stone, and the detail that it sunk is the narrator's way of saying the matter was finished before Goliath hit the ground. The word marks other finished things. Jeremiah was let down with cords into a dungeon with no water but mire, “so Jeremiah sunk in the mire” (Jer 38:6) — a faithful prophet at the bottom of a cistern for telling the truth, and rescued by an Ethiopian eunuch with old cast clouts and rotten rags for his armholes. Zedekiah is warned that his own feet “are sunk in the mire” (Jer 38:22) by the friends who set him on. The psalmist sees the judgment that fits: “The heathen are sunk down in the pit that they made: in the net which they hid is their own foot taken” (Psa 9:15). And Luke, with a physician's honesty about a long sermon, records that Eutychus “sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead” (Act 20:9) — and Paul went down and embraced him, and they brought the young man alive.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sink as to fall by the force of gravity, to descend below the surface, to settle down; and figuratively, to be overwhelmed or depressed.
webster_full: SINK, v.i. To fall by the force of greater gravity, in a medium or substance of less specific gravity; to subside; opposed to swim or float.
1. To fall gradually; to descend; as, the sun sinks in the west.
2. To enter deeply; to be impressed; as, let these sayings sink down into your ears.
3. To be overwhelmed or depressed; as, the heart sinks under sorrow.
scriptures: And David put his hand in his bag, and took thence a stone, and slang it, and smote the Philistine in his forehead, that the stone sunk into his forehead; and he fell upon his face to the earth.
Jer 38:6

Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire.
Psa 9:15
The heathen are sunk down in the pit that they made: in the net which they hid is their own foot taken.
Act 20:9

And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The verb is plain, and its biblical uses are narrative rather than doctrinal.

The principle to recover is that faithfulness is not always visibly rewarded in the moment, and that the reader should not read Jeremiah 38:6 and 1 Samuel 17:49 as though they were the same kind of story. David's stone sank and he was made a captain; Jeremiah sank in the mire for saying what God had told him to say, and the mire was the reward of the ministry. Both are in the same Book and both are the will of God for the man in them. Psalm 9:15 supplies the long view — the pit-diggers fall into their own pits, and the net taken is their own foot — but the psalm does not promise it will happen on a schedule the sufferer can see from the bottom of a cistern.
roots_summary: Hebrew taba' (H2883), to sink, to be settled or fixed in; shaqa'; Greek katapherō (G2702), to be borne down.
roots_lines: Hebrew taba' (H2883) — to sink, to settle down into; 1 Samuel 17:49 (the stone into the forehead), Jeremiah 38:6, 38:22, Psalm 9:15.
Hebrew tit (H2916) — mire, clay; the dungeon Jeremiah sank in, and Psalm 40:2, the miry clay God brought David up out of.
Hebrew shachath (H7845) — a pit, a trap dug for another; Psalm 9:15.
Greek katapherō (G2702) — to be borne down, to be overcome (by sleep); Acts 20:9, twice in one verse.
Greek hupnos bathus (G5258) — a deep sleep; the condition Eutychus fell into in the window.

“So Jeremiah sunk in the mire” — the reward of a faithful ministry.
“Sunk down in the pit that they made” — their own foot in their own net.

pos: v. (bound, fastened; of a lace, of kine, of horses, and of the colt at the door)
etymology: Saxon tigan, to bind. The word's great use is in the entry into Jerusalem, where four of its seven occurrences fall on one animal.
biblical_def: “Go into the village over against you, and straightway ye shall find an ass tied, and a colt with her: loose them, and bring them unto me” (Mat 21:2). Mark, Luke and Matthew all record the tied colt, and all record the instruction to loose it; Mark adds the detail that they “found the colt tied by the door without in a place where two ways met” (Mar 11:4). Every particular had been foreseen — the village, the animal, the fact that never man sat on it, the owners standing by, and the words that would satisfy them: the Lord hath need of him. Zechariah had said the King would come lowly, riding upon an ass, and He came on a borrowed unbroken colt that had to be untied first. The other uses are quiet and worth keeping. Bezaleel's craftsmen “tied unto it a lace of blue, to fasten it on high upon the mitre; as the LORD commanded Moses” (Exo 39:31) — the golden plate HOLINESS TO THE LORD secured to the high priest's head by a blue lace. The Philistines “took two milch kine, and tied them to the cart” (1Sa 6:10), separated from their calves, and the cows went lowing straight up the road to Bethshemesh against every instinct. And the lepers at Samaria found the Syrian camp abandoned, “horses tied, and asses tied, and the tents as they were” (2Ki 7:10) — an army fled from a sound God had made.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tie as to bind, to fasten with a cord or band; to unite so as not to be easily parted; and tied as bound or fastened.
webster_full: TIE, v.t. To bind; to fasten with a band or cord and knot.
1. To fasten; to hold; as, the parties are tied by the contract.
2. To unite so as not to be easily parted.
3. To confine; to restrain from liberty.
TIED, pp. Fastened with a knot; bound; united.
scriptures: Mat 21:2
Saying unto them, Go into the village over against you, and straightway ye shall find an ass tied, and a colt with her: loose them, and bring them unto me.
Mar 11:4
And they went their way, and found the colt tied by the door without in a place where two ways met; and they loose him.
And they tied unto it a lace of blue, to fasten it on high upon the mitre; as the LORD commanded Moses.

So they came and called unto the porter of the city: and they told them, saying, We came to the camp of the Syrians, and, behold, there was no man there, neither voice of man, but horses tied, and asses tied, and the tents as they were.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The verb is ordinary and carries no contested freight.

The principle to recover is the precision of prophecy fulfilled in small things. Our Lord sent two disciples to a village with a description exact enough to be checked — an ass and a colt, tied, at a door where two ways met, whereon never man sat — and a sentence to say if anyone objected. Zechariah 9:9 had named the manner of the King's coming five centuries earlier. Providence had arranged an unbroken colt to be standing tied at that particular door on that particular morning, and had prepared its owners to let it go. The believer who trusts God with the large outlines and doubts Him over the details of a week has the proportion exactly backwards; Scripture's God is most impressive in the small print.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'asar (H631), to bind, to tie, to harness; pathil (H6616), a cord or lace; Greek deo (G1210), to bind; luo (G3089), to loose.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'asar (H631) — to bind, tie, harness; 1 Samuel 6:10, 2 Kings 7:10.
Hebrew pathil (H6616) — a cord, thread, lace; Exodus 39:31, the lace of blue that held the holy crown to the mitre.
Hebrew tekeleth (H8504) — blue; the colour of the lace, and of the ribband on the fringe of every Israelite's garment.
Greek deo (G1210) — to bind, to tie; Matthew 21:2, Mark 11:2-4, Luke 19:30.
Greek luo (G3089) — to loose, to untie; the command given four times over the same colt — loose him, and bring him.
usage: “Ye shall find an ass tied, and a colt with her: loose them”.
“Tied by the door without in a place where two ways met”.
“They tied unto it a lace of blue” — HOLINESS TO THE LORD, upon the mitre.

pos: n. and v. (the iron of a bridle put in a horse's mouth; and the past tense of bite)
etymology: Saxon bitan, to bite — a bit being what is bitten upon. The Authorized Version uses both senses, and the two together supply the psalm's picture of a man who must be governed by force because he would not be led by counsel.
biblical_def: “Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle, lest they come near unto thee” (Psa 32:9). The verse comes immediately after the promise, I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye. Two forms of government are set side by side: the eye, which requires a creature attentive enough to be looking at its master's face, and the bit, which requires only a mouth. God will have His way with His children either way, and David — who had lately been brought back by the harder method — is urging the easier. Guidance by the eye is not for the spiritually elite; it is simply the alternative to being handled like a mule. The verb supplies the other two occurrences, and both are about a bite that comes from where a man was not looking. “The LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died” (Num 21:6) — the plague that produced the brazen serpent, and the type our Lord applied to Himself in John 3:14. And Amos: “As if a man did flee from a lion, and a bear met him; or went into the house, and leaned his hand on the wall, and a serpent bit him” (Amo 5:19) — the day of the LORD for those who desired it, with no safe wall to lean on.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bit as the iron part of a bridle which is inserted in the mouth of a horse, with its appendages; and bite as to break or crush with the teeth.
webster_full: BIT, n. In a general sense, a small piece; the part of a bridle which is inserted in the mouth of a horse.
1. A small piece of any thing; a mouthful; a morsel.
BITE, v.t. To break or crush with the teeth, as in eating; to pierce with the teeth, as a serpent.
BRIDLE, n. The instrument with which a horse is governed and restrained by a rider.
scriptures: Psa 32:9
Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle, lest they come near unto thee.
Num 21:6
And the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.
Amo 5:19
As if a man did flee from a lion, and a bear met him; or went into the house, and leaned his hand on the wall, and a serpent bit him.
corruption_summary: Restraint is treated as an assault on the self; the psalm treats it as the fallback for a creature that would not be led by the eye.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning anthropology holds that the authentic self is the unrestrained self, and that discipline — parental, ecclesiastical, or self-imposed — is an imposition on it. Psalm 32:9 begins somewhere else. Restraint is not the enemy of the creature; it is the fallback when the gentler government has been refused. The horse and the mule are not condemned for being restrained but for having no understanding, so that nothing but a bit will serve. The believer is offered guidance by the eye, and the eye can only guide a face that is turned toward it.

The place of the verse in the psalm matters. Psalm 32 is a psalm of forgiveness — blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven — written by a man who had spent a season with God's hand heavy upon him day and night until he confessed. He knows the bit from the inside. His counsel to others is therefore not the advice of a man who has never needed restraining but of one who has felt the bridle and would spare his readers the experience. That is how Christian exhortation usually earns its authority.

“Leaned his hand on the wall, and a serpent bit him” — no safe wall in that day.

pos: adj. (made of wool; in the law, one of the two fibres that might not be mingled in a garment)
etymology: From wool, Saxon wull. In the law of Moses woollen is always named beside linen, and the pairing is the point: an animal fibre and a vegetable fibre, which Israel was forbidden to weave into one cloth.
biblical_def: “Thou shalt not wear a garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together” (Deu 22:11), and in Leviticus among the statutes of separation: “neither shall a garment mingled of linen and woollen come upon thee” (Lev 19:19), set beside not letting cattle gender with a diverse kind and not sowing a field with mingled seed. These are the boundary statutes. They taught a people, by the clothes on their backs and the seed in their fields, that God had separated them and that holiness has edges. Notably the priests' garments and the tabernacle hangings did combine the fibres — the mixture was reserved to the sanctuary and forbidden to the common Israelite, which sharpened rather than blurred the lesson. The other four occurrences are the law of the fretting leprosy in a garment: “The garment also that the plague of leprosy is in, whether it be a woollen garment, or a linen garment” (Lev 13:47), examined in the warp or the woof, shut up seven days, and if the plague spread, “He shall therefore burn that garment… for it is a fretting leprosy; it shall be burnt in the fire” (Lev 13:52). A plague that could live in cloth had to be burned, not laundered. The ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ and no longer binds the conscience as to fibre; what abides is the doctrine it taught — that the holy and the common are not to be mingled thoughtlessly, and that some corruptions must be destroyed rather than managed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines woollen as made of wool, consisting of wool, pertaining to wool; and wool as the soft curled hair which grows on sheep and some other animals.
webster_full: WOOLLEN, a. Made of wool; consisting of wool; as woollen cloth.
1. Pertaining to wool; as woollen manufactures.
WOOL, n. That soft species of hair which grows on sheep and some other animals, which in fineness sometimes approaches to fur.
LINEN, n. Cloth made of flax or hemp.
scriptures: Thou shalt not wear a garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together.

Ye shall keep my statutes. Thou shalt not let thy cattle gender with a diverse kind: thou shalt not sow thy field with mingled seed: neither shall a garment mingled of linen and woollen come upon thee.
The garment also that the plague of leprosy is in, whether it be a woollen garment, or a linen garment;
He shall therefore burn that garment, whether warp or woof, in woollen or in linen, or any thing of skin, wherein the plague is: for it is a fretting leprosy; it shall be burnt in the fire.
corruption_summary: The mingled-fibre law is produced as proof that Scripture's moral commands may be discarded too; the threefold division of the law answers it.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 19:19 is the favourite exhibit of those arguing that a Christian who eats shellfish and wears blended cloth has no standing to cite Leviticus 18 or 20 on sexual morality. The answer is not a dodge but the historic Reformed reading of the law, set out in LBCF 19: God gave Israel ceremonial laws, which prefigured Christ and are now abrogated; judicial laws, which expired with that state and bind only in their general equity; and the moral law, summarized in the ten commandments, which binds all men in all ages. The mingled garment is ceremonial — a visible schoolmaster teaching separation. The prohibitions of Leviticus 18 are moral, are grounded on the creation order rather than on Israel's calendar, are applied to the surrounding nations who had no ceremonial law at all, and are reaffirmed in the New Testament (Rom 1; 1Co 6:9-11).

The abiding principle in these statutes is real and should not be surrendered along with the fibre. God's people were taught holiness through their clothing, their fields and their herds, so that no part of ordinary life was outside the question of whether it belonged to Him. And the leprous garment adds a hard mercy: some things are not to be cleaned but burned. The Christian who keeps negotiating with a besetting sin, laundering it season after season, is refusing what Leviticus 13:52 says plainly — a fretting plague in the cloth means the cloth goes into the fire.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsemer (H6785), wool; pishteh (H6593), linen, flax; sha'atnez (H8162), a mixed fabric of wool and linen.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsemer (H6785) — wool; Leviticus 13:47-59, 19:19, Deuteronomy 22:11.
Hebrew pishteh (H6593) — flax, linen; always paired with wool in these statutes.
Hebrew sha'atnez (H8162) — a fabric of mixed stuff, wool and linen woven together; Leviticus 19:19, Deuteronomy 22:11 — the technical name for the forbidden cloth.

Hebrew mam'ereth (H3992) — fretting, malignant; Leviticus 13:52, a fretting leprosy that must be burnt.
usage: “A garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together” — forbidden to the common man.
“Whether it be a woollen garment, or a linen garment” — the plague examined in the cloth.
“It is a fretting leprosy; it shall be burnt in the fire” — not laundered.
